question.text: What is the difference between a 'wire transfer originator' information requirement for cross-border transfers versus domestic transfers?

answer.text: Cross-border transfers require originator and beneficiary identifiers, with additional originator address/ID/date-place details at USD 1000 or more; domestic transfers may carry only the originator account or reference number provided it is traceable and full information is supplied within required timelines or immediately to law enforcement
There is no difference — both require exactly the same information
Domestic transfers require more information than cross-border transfers because of stricter local regulations
Cross-border transfers do not require any originator information because the beneficiary bank handles all verification

explanation.text: The Logic: Under the IFSCA Guidelines, cross-border wire transfers must carry originator and beneficiary identifiers, with additional originator details (address, national ID number, or date and place of birth) required when the transfer is USD 1,000 or more. Domestic transfers may carry only the originator's account number or a unique reference number, provided the transaction remains traceable and full originator/beneficiary information is made available within required timelines or immediately on request to law enforcement and supervisory authorities. The Trap: Option B is tempting because both types do require some originator information, but cross-border and domestic regimes differ on what must accompany the message versus what may be supplied on request, and the USD 1,000 threshold triggers expanded cross-border requirements. Note: For cross-border wire transfers of USD 1,000 or more, ensure complete originator and beneficiary information is included; for domestic transfers, ensure the reference number used can be linked back to full underlying records on demand.
